criteria.name: Story stands alone without external paratext
criteria.instruction: Judge whether the story is complete and comprehensible using only the text given, versus depending on embedded links to the author's other posts, references to an ongoing personal saga/continuity, or footer plugs to feel complete or land its appeal. High: no fact needed to understand the story is missing from the text itself. Low: the piece leans on 'this is part of an ongoing saga,' hyperlinked backstory, or a subreddit plug to feel finished.
criteria.rationale: R02 is explicitly 'story #1385 in a row' in an 'ongoing saga,' with several embedded hyperlinks substituting for on-page worldbuilding; R08 is marked 'a continuation of a series of earlier prompt responses' with a linked precursor needed for full context. Both score card_high/dense_low (.850/.027 and .865/.093) -- the scorecard does not appear to discount reliance on paratext the way the dense reader, who can't see the linked material, does.

criteria.name: Implicit Worldbuilding
criteria.instruction: Score high when institutions, customs, history, and rules emerge through behavior, objects, and constraints rather than explanatory summary; score low when the story supplies lore without dramatizing its consequences.
criteria.rationale: R08 and R13 reveal entire social systems through their customs and institutional reactions, while R03 often explains its mythology directly instead of embodying it.

criteria.name: Controlled Repetition and Rhythm
criteria.instruction: Score high when repeated words, structures, or images accumulate changing meaning and regulate pace; score low when repetition is accidental, ornamental, or merely redundant.
criteria.rationale: R01’s recurring service refrain changes from doctrine to mourning, and R32’s counting pattern formally enacts the narrator’s temporal disorientation.

criteria.name: Ending reframes what preceded rather than announcing closure
criteria.instruction: Score 0-4 on the final beat. 4 = the last lines send the reader back through the story with changed understanding, using material planted earlier, and the reframing is not stated as a conclusion. 2 = a clean, correct resolution that adds no new reading. 0 = the ending states the moral, the emotion, or the lesson learned, OR introduces a frame in the last line that nothing earlier prepared. Both failures should be scored 0: the announced ending and the arbitrary rug-pull are the same defect, an ending that does not arise from the body of the story.
criteria.rationale: R04 plants a secret fear in one withheld sentence and pays it off in four final words - 'I would have to fly' - which recolours the whole hatching, including the narrator's suppressed hope that the egg had died. R37 answers all three of the prompt's questions at once in a subordinate clause about interbreeding with or eliminating near-peer species. Against these, R25 arrives at 'I've gotta stop gambling' with nothing behind it, and R03 closes by telling us hope was not over after all. The two announced or arbitrary endings are scorecard-high; the two reframing endings are scorecard-bottom, which suggests the bank credits the presence of a twist or a resolution rather than its preparation.

criteria.name: Voice With Control
criteria.instruction: Score high when diction, syntax, figurative language, and narrative distance consistently express a distinctive consciousness while serving the scene; score low when voice is generic or consists mainly of a repeated mannerism.
criteria.rationale: R25’s unstable cosmic language and R34’s formal collective voice are inseparable from their narrators, unlike the largely mannerism-driven dialect in R06.

criteria.name: Interest built by the story, not borrowed from known material
criteria.instruction: Score 0-4. 4 = characters, world, and jokes generate their own specificity; where the piece uses a familiar genre or pre-existing characters (which some prompts explicitly require), it supplies a pressure, perception or consequence those sources do not already supply. 2 = competent use of a known register with one original element. 0 = the piece runs on recognition - stock components assembled in the expected order, or imported characters whose entire charge is pre-existing and whose meeting merely confirms what a reader already knows about each. Do not penalize a crossover or a genre exercise for being one; penalize it for adding nothing.
criteria.rationale: R23 flags its own cliche in passing - the narrator finds the single dangling lightbulb a bit cliche - and then plays every other one straight: the phonetically accented interrogator, the defiant wisecracks, the femme fatale rescue with a pistol from the blouse. R06 assembles the noir kit in sequence: tacky Hawaiian shirt, devoted secretary, the ex-wife, the young dame in trouble with a gangster's necklace, the baby blues just like Cece. R38 lets Chigurh and Joffrey carry the whole load; the encounter ends where a reader's prior knowledge of both would predict. All three are scorecard-high. Against them, R19 takes the same prompt-genre and invents a supervillain whose actual power is municipal planning, and lands near the scorecard's floor.

criteria.name: Reaches real closure rather than an excerpt hook
criteria.instruction: Judge whether the piece reaches an actual ending -- a beginning, complication, and resolution (even a dark or ambiguous one) contained within the text -- versus functioning as an opening or excerpt of a longer work, ending on a hook, a cliffhanger mid-reveal, or a scene-setting line that promises a story not yet begun. High: something has changed and settled by the final line. Low: the final line exists to launch a story the text doesn't actually contain.
criteria.rationale: R32 reaches a complete, self-contained shock ending within a few short paragraphs (dense_high/card_low .943/.030). Contrast with R40, card_high/dense_low (.815/.050), whose story ends on 'Just got back from vacation' -- a line setting up a detective case the text hasn't started (its footer's crossed-out word count also flags it as a truncated/serialized excerpt) -- and R09, also card_high/dense_low (.897/.054), which ends mid-cliffhanger on the villain's taunt with no resolution at all.

criteria.name: Non-Obvious Consequence
criteria.instruction: Score high when the premise leads to a surprising consequence or choice that is nevertheless psychologically and causally credible; score low when the story merely lists familiar trope ingredients or performs a shallow inversion.
criteria.rationale: R10 turns universal infection into emotional extinction, R16 turns legal victory into enforced silence, and R27 finds a conceptual consequence inside the classroom joke.

criteria.name: Detail that does work versus decorative inventory
criteria.instruction: Score 0-4 on what the concrete particulars accomplish. 4 = the specifics imply expertise, economy, danger or social position that the story never states, and deleting them would cost the reader real knowledge. 2 = accurate detail that establishes setting and no more. 0 = nouns catalogued for texture - brands, furnishings, colours, equipment lists - which could be deleted or substituted without any change to what the reader understands. Test each cluster of detail by asking what the reader now knows that they could not have guessed from the prompt.
criteria.rationale: R04 implies an entire trained practice - feeding the arm through the harness to widen it, gripping the traces, taking her down to a knee, sitting her until she stops struggling - and thereby the sixteen generations of family the story asserts only once. R11 makes the family's survival margin arithmetic rather than adjective: half the crop failed, half of the rest only now ripening, enough to cover seed and equipment repairs and winter food and nothing else. Against these, R02 walks its room item by item - vivid blue carpet, racecar bed, silver macbook, 32 inch flat screen, Apple TV - and none of it tells the reader anything the phrase 'childlike bedroom' would not. R02 is near the scorecard ceiling, R04 and R11 near its floor, so the bank appears to be counting sensory density rather than weighing what the density buys.

criteria.name: Compression With Narrative Payoff
criteria.instruction: Score high when a short or highly selective story efficiently establishes context, character, movement, and payoff; score low when brevity produces a sketch or when length adds little usable information.
criteria.rationale: R26 compresses an alien-homecoming reversal into a compact poem, whereas R29 compresses its premise into a single gag without meaningful development.

criteria.name: Premise as a Causal Engine
criteria.instruction: Score high when the prompt’s unusual premise directly causes characters’ choices, conflicts, and events; score low when it merely decorates an otherwise generic scene.
criteria.rationale: R07 makes universal infection drive social and biological consequences, while R09 mainly explains whale institutions around a loosely developing conflict.

criteria.name: Escalation Through Consequence
criteria.instruction: Score high when each development narrows options or creates a harder subsequent problem; score low when events accumulate without materially changing what characters can do.
criteria.rationale: R34 moves from routine security work to a concealed massacre, while R06 reaches possession quickly but stops before developing its consequences.

criteria.name: Dialogue With Subtext
criteria.instruction: Score high when speakers pursue different immediate aims, avoid stating the central issue directly, and reveal relationships through wording and interruption; score low when dialogue only explains the premise or trades interchangeable quips.
criteria.rationale: The exchanges in R18 and R28 conceal power and care beneath casual language, whereas R03’s conversations mainly deliver rules and backstory.

criteria.name: Self-Implication in Character Desire
criteria.instruction: Score high when a protagonist’s goal exposes their own contradiction, weakness, or complicity; score low when characters simply pursue an externally stated objective.
criteria.rationale: R24 makes Mason’s dependence and jealousy part of the central problem, and R40 openly examines the ego behind supposedly charitable behavior.

criteria.name: Form matches and amplifies content
criteria.instruction: Judge whether the story's structural form (verse, an unbroken dialogue-only scene, fragmented interior monologue, essay-like exposition, etc.) is a deliberate choice that does communicative work, versus defaulting to conventional linear prose-scene structure regardless of content. High: the form itself carries meaning -- e.g., a poem whose rhyme/meter lands the story's turn, or a piece built entirely from one dialogue exchange that reveals character through the exchange alone. Low: the story could be re-typeset as ordinary paragraph narration and lose nothing; the form is generic and unconsidered.
criteria.rationale: Explains why the dense model rates R01 (told entirely as rhyming verse) and R04 (told entirely as one unbroken Socratic classroom dialogue) very highly (dense_pct .967 and .945) while the scorecard rates both near the bottom (card_pct .083 and .081) -- a checklist of generic prose-craft items (setting, description, pacing) has no natural slot for 'form itself as content.' R28's fragmented, clipped-sentence prose-poem style (dense_pct .986, card_pct .130) shows the same pattern.

criteria.name: Self-promotional sign-off naming the author's own subreddit or handle
criteria.instruction: Count the promotional apparatus attached to the story that points the reader at the writer rather than at this story: a bare handle or personal-subreddit line, 'thanks for reading', 'check out my other stories', an invitation to follow or subscribe. HIGH = an explicit sign-off block with a handle, personal subreddit, or solicitation to read more. LOW = the text ends on its last narrative sentence with nothing appended.
criteria.upstream_parent: an established personal following / author brand inside the community
criteria.rationale: R32 closes 'Thanks for reading! I have a couple of popular stories ... at r/AuthorKurt'; R38 closes 'I've got much better stories at r/BLT_WITH_RANCH'; R19 signs 'r/AinsleyAdams'; R01 signs 'r/dexdrafts'; R15 closes 'be sure to check out my subreddit for more of my writing'. A writer who owns a personal subreddit already has readers who arrive for the byline. It is a suspected-spurious channel rather than an arm marker: it shows up on both sides of the slice (R01/R19/R32/R38 dense-high, R15/R35 dense-low), so it is doing work orthogonal to what either model is reading. Mixed because a writer with a following usually has volume and practice behind them.

criteria.name: Series-continuity residue
criteria.instruction: Count explicit continuation notes, recurring-universe references, returning characters, installment numbers, or links to prior episodes. High degree means substantial serial residue; low degree means a self-contained entry.
criteria.rationale: R24 identifies a numbered daily saga and connects several recurring characters, while R39 explicitly calls itself a continuation. Series familiarity may affect reception independently, although sustained serial writing can also improve craft.

criteria.name: Non-standard spelling/grammar slips (unedited-draft marker)
criteria.instruction: Count clear misspellings, malapropisms, or grammar slips that a spellchecker or a single editing pass would have caught (e.g. a wrong word substituted, letters transposed, a homophone confused). HIGH = multiple such slips are visible in the running text. LOW = clean, edited-looking prose with no obvious slips.
criteria.upstream_parent: whether the writer had editing help, used a spellchecker, or gave the piece a revision pass before posting (a proxy for a more professional/experienced production process)
criteria.rationale: R08 contains 'reproductive sistem' and 'posseses' for 'system'/'possesses', and R39 (which explicitly flags itself as a first-time poster) contains 'aliean', 'exestential', 'preverbial', and 'ceentury'. These slips are a visible trace of a first-draft, unedited production process rather than a professional or heavily revised one. Mixed:true because an author with editing help or more experience is also plausibly a stronger prose stylist overall, so the same upstream cause -- editing access or experience -- could genuinely correlate with better writing, not just fewer typos.

criteria.name: Event-participation markers
criteria.instruction: Count challenge labels, heat or round identifiers, theme-event names, participant tags, host thanks, and competition-oriented closing notes. High means strong event packaging; low means ordinary standalone presentation.
criteria.rationale: Participation in organized community events can alter visibility and reader expectations without improving the text. R21 is framed as Theme Thursday and tags another user; R30 names a competition round and thanks its organizers; R39 includes Theme Thursday and a participant tag.

criteria.name: Fragmented staccato paragraphing / line-break repetition
criteria.instruction: Count the fraction of paragraphs that are a single short clause or sentence (under roughly eight words) set off by its own line break, and note literal repetition of a short phrase (e.g. counting patterns, repeated single words). HIGH = the story is built mostly from such isolated one-line beats. LOW = paragraphs are built from ordinary multi-sentence prose units.
criteria.rationale: R02 ('1, 2, 3. 1, 2, 3.' ... 'No more. No more.') and R20 ('I stare in the mirror, and sigh. / I am paler...') both rely on this staccato, one-line-per-beat texture and both sit in dense_high/card_low. The typographic choppiness can read as 'raw interiority' to a model perceiving overall shape, but it is a cheap formatting trick any writer can apply regardless of what is actually being said.

criteria.name: Immediate voice opening
criteria.instruction: Score how strongly the opening begins with first-person narration in present tense and/or direct dialogue before establishing broader context. High means an immediate voiced opening; low means delayed, descriptive, or retrospective exposition.
criteria.rationale: A fashionable opening mode can shape first impressions independently of later story quality. R09 begins with urgent dialogue and present-tense action, R23 opens inside a first-person present workplace scene, and R36 starts with rapid dialogue.

criteria.name: Borrowed recognisable characters or franchises doing the characterisation
criteria.instruction: Count named entities the story takes from outside itself - film, TV, game, canonical religious or mythic figures - and judge how much of the scene's weight rests on reader-supplied knowledge of them. HIGH = the central figures are pre-existing properties who arrive fully characterised and the story spends no words building them. LOW = every character is invented for this story and established on the page.
criteria.upstream_parent: pre-existing audience attachment to a franchise or figure; fandom pull that operates before the prose is read
criteria.rationale: R08 runs entirely on two imported canons (Anton Chigurh's coin toss confronting Joffrey Baratheon) and never has to establish either man; R31 places Freddy Krueger in a bedroom and lets the name do the irony; R40 fields Gabriel and Beelzebub; R16 uses the messiah as a roommate. The recognisability is free labour the writer did not perform. Not mixed - borrowing a beloved figure supplies affection without supplying craft.

criteria.name: Markup punctuation density
criteria.instruction: Count visible italics, bold, all-caps emphasis, em-dashes, ellipses, dividers, underscores, and other conspicuous typographic devices. High degree means frequent decorative emphasis; low degree means mostly plain prose.
criteria.rationale: R03 combines italics, bold text, and a long divider, while R19 uses italicized thoughts, repeated dashes, and an ornamental closing. These signals may guide genre or tone expectations without proving the story is better.

criteria.name: Proper-noun token count
criteria.instruction: Count how many capitalised proper nouns (names of people, places, organisations, invented terms) the story uses. Score 1.0 for a very high count, 0.5 for a moderate count, 0.0 for few or none. Count the capitalised tokens only; pay no attention to whether the world they name is coherent or conveyed well.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow lexical counterpart of R4A02 'Implicit Worldbuilding': proper-noun density is the surface residue of an invented world while measuring nothing about whether the world is revealed through consequence rather than announcement.

criteria.name: Repeated-phrase exact-match count
criteria.instruction: Count how many word sequences of three or more words appear more than once in the story, verbatim. Score 1.0 when several such repeats occur, 0.5 for one or two, 0.0 for none. Count exact string repeats only; pay no attention to whether any repetition is deliberate or does rhetorical work.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow string-matching counterpart of R4A03 'Controlled Repetition and Rhythm': it counts literal repeats while measuring nothing about control or rhythm, and would score an accidental verbal tic identically to a refrain.
